newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds close firmer after Martin speech.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds close firmer after Martin speech.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed in firmer territory on Wednesday, after Finance Minister Paul Martin reported a lower federal government deficit for 1995/96 as expected by many market players.

Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.10 to C$106.30 to yield 7.451 percent, compared to the U.S. 30-year benchmark which fell 11/32 to yield 6.83 percent. The spread between the two narrowed to 62 basis points from 66 at Tuesday's close.
Martin led his update to the House of Commons Finance Committee with the news that Canada's budget deficit was C$28.6 billion in 1995/96, down from a projected C$32.7 billion.
Martin also forecast a 1998/99 deficit of C$9.0 billion or about one percent of gross domestic product, and said a broad-based tax cut now would be wrong.

"I think his insistence that he won't cut taxes strengthens the market's view of the government's resolve to stay the course," said Michael Manford, chief economist with Scotia Capital Markets. "It's also very bullish for the Canadian dollar."
Spreads between Canada-U.S. bonds yields at the 30-year level are now at their lowest point in 11 years, breaking a record set on Monday.
The rally in Canadian fixed-income markets was tempered by the fact that investors earlier this week had already begun to price good news into bonds and T-bills.
In new issue news, the Province of Ontario this morning set a C$500 million 7.6 percent bond due June 2, 2027 in the Canadian market, said lead manager ScotiaMcLeod Inc.
The issue was priced at C$98.539 to yield 7.724 percent for a spread of 31 basis points above the Government of Canada's 8.0 percent bond due June, 2023.
In other prices, the Government of Canada 7.0 percent of 2006 rose C$0.34 to C$101.59 to yield 6.779 percent.
The U.S. 10-year benchmark fell 3/32 to yield 6.55 percent.
The spread between the two benchmark bonds dropped to 23 basis points from 27 basis points at Tuesday's close. The spread between the bonds is also now at an 11-year low.
The three-month cash bill traded at 3.46 percent against the U.S. three-month bill at 5.12 percent.
